message.content:
You are a knowledge compiler. Your job is to read a daily conversation log
and extract knowledge into structured wiki articles.

## Schema (AGENTS.md)

# AGENTS.md - Personal Knowledge Base Schema

> Adapted from [Andrej Karpathy's LLM Knowledge Base](https://gist.github.com/karpathy/442a6bf555914893e9891c11519de94f) architecture.
> Instead of ingesting external articles, this system compiles knowledge from your own AI conversations.

## The Compiler Analogy

```
daily/          = source code    (your conversations - the raw material)
LLM             = compiler       (extracts and organizes knowledge)
knowledge/      = executable     (structured, queryable knowledge base)
lint            = test suite     (health checks for consistency)
memlint         = test suite     (same, for the memory files loaded each session)
queries         = runtime        (using the knowledge)
```

You don't manually organize your knowledge. You have conversations, and the LLM handles the synthesis, cross-referencing, and maintenance.

---

## Architecture

### Layer 1: `daily/` - Conversation Logs (Immutable Source)

Daily logs capture what happened in your AI coding sessions. These are the "raw sources" - append-only, never edited after the fact.

```
daily/
├── 2026-04-01.md
├── 2026-04-02.md
├── ...
```

Each file follows this format:

```markdown
# Daily Log: YYYY-MM-DD

## Sessions

### Session (HH:MM) - Brief Title

**Context:** What the user was working on.

**Key Exchanges:**
- User asked about X, assistant explained Y
- Decided to use Z approach because...
- Discovered that W doesn't work when...

**Decisions Made:**
- Chose library X over Y because...
- Architecture: went with pattern Z

**Lessons Learned:**
- Always do X before Y to avoid...
- The gotcha with Z is that...

**Action Items:**
- [ ] Follow up on X
- [ ] Refactor Y when time permits
```

### Layer 2: `knowledge/` - Compiled Knowledge (LLM-Owned)

The LLM owns this directory entirely. Humans read it but rarely edit it directly.

```
knowledge/
├── index.md              # Master catalog - every article with one-line summary
├── log.md                # Append-only chronological build log
├── concepts/             # Atomic knowledge articles
├── connections/          # Cross-cutting insights linking 2+ concepts
└── qa/                   # Filed query answers (compounding knowledge)
```

### Layer 3: This File (AGENTS.md)

The schema that tells the LLM how to compile and maintain the knowledge base. This is the "compiler specification."

---

## Structural Files

### `knowledge/index.md` - Master Catalog

A table listing every knowledge article. This is the primary retrieval mechanism - the LLM reads this FIRST when answering any query, then selects relevant articles to read in full.

Format:

```markdown
# Knowledge Base Index

| Article | Summary | Compiled From | Updated |
|---------|---------|---------------|---------|
| [[concepts/supabase-auth]] | Row-level security patterns and JWT gotchas | daily/2026-04-02.md | 2026-04-02 |
| [[connections/auth-and-webhooks]] | Token verification patterns shared across Supabase auth and Stripe webhooks | daily/2026-04-02.md, daily/2026-04-04.md | 2026-04-04 |
```

### `knowledge/log.md` - Build Log

Append-only chronological record of every compile, query, and lint operation.

Format:

```markdown
# Build Log

## [2026-04-01T14:30:00] compile | Daily Log 2026-04-01
- Source: daily/2026-04-01.md
- Articles created: [[concepts/nextjs-project-structure]], [[concepts/tailwind-setup]]
- Articles updated: (none)

## [2026-04-02T09:00:00] query | "How do I handle auth redirects?"
- Consulted: [[concepts/supabase-auth]], [[concepts/nextjs-middleware]]
- Filed to: [[qa/auth-redirect-handling]]
```

---

## Article Formats

### Concept Articles (`knowledge/concepts/`)

One article per atomic piece of knowledge. These are facts, patterns, decisions, preferences, and lessons extracted from your conversations.

```markdown
---
title: "Concept Name"
aliases: [alternate-name, abbreviation]
tags: [domain, topic]
sources:
  - "daily/2026-04-01.md"
  - "daily/2026-04-03.md"
created: 2026-04-01
updated: 2026-04-03
---

# Concept Name

[2-4 sentence core explanation]

## Key Points

- [Bullet points, each self-contained]

## Details

[Deeper explanation, encyclopedia-style paragraphs]

## Related Concepts

- [[concepts/related-concept]] - How it connects

## Sources

- [[daily/2026-04-01.md]] - Initial discovery during project setup
- [[daily/2026-04-03.md]] - Updated after debugging session
```

### Connection Articles (`knowledge/connections/`)

Cross-cutting synthesis linking 2+ concepts. Created when a conversation reveals a non-obvious relationship.

```markdown
---
title: "Connection: X and Y"
connects:
  - "concepts/concept-x"
  - "concepts/concept-y"
sources:
  - "daily/2026-04-04.md"
created: 2026-04-04
updated: 2026-04-04
---

# Connection: X and Y

## The Connection

[What links these concepts]

## Key Insight

[The non-obvious relationship discovered]

## Evidence

[Specific examples from conversations]

## Related Concepts

- [[concepts/concept-x]]
- [[concepts/concept-y]]
```

### Q&A Articles (`knowledge/qa/`)

Filed answers from queries. Every complex question answered by the system can be permanently stored, making future queries smarter.

```markdown
---
title: "Q: Original Question"
question: "The exact question asked"
consulted:
  - "concepts/article-1"
  - "concepts/article-2"
filed: 2026-04-05
---

# Q: Original Question

## Answer

[The synthesized answer with [[wikilinks]] to sources]

## Sources Consulted

- [[concepts/article-1]] - Relevant because...
- [[concepts/article-2]] - Provided context on...

## Follow-Up Questions

- What about edge case X?
- How does this change if Y?
```

---

## Core Operations

### 1. Compile (daily/ -> knowledge/)

When processing a daily log:

1. Read the daily log file
2. Read `knowledge/index.md` to understand current knowledge state
3. Read existing articles that may need updating
4. For each piece of knowledge found in the log:
   - If an existing concept article covers this topic: UPDATE it with new information, add the daily log as a source
   - If it's a new topic: CREATE a new `concepts/` article
5. If the log reveals a non-obvious connection between 2+ existing concepts: CREATE a `connections/` article
6. UPDATE `knowledge/index.md` with new/modified entries
7. APPEND to `knowledge/log.md`

**Important guidelines:**
- A single daily log may touch 3-10 knowledge articles
- Prefer updating existing articles over creating near-duplicates
- Use Obsidian-style `[[wikilinks]]` with full relative paths from knowledge/
- Write in encyclopedia style - factual, concise, self-contained
- Every article must have YAML frontmatter
- Every article must link back to its source daily logs

### 2. Query (Ask the Knowledge Base)

1. Read `knowledge/index.md` (the master catalog)
2. Based on the question, identify 3-10 relevant articles from the index
3. Read those articles in full
4. Synthesize an answer with `[[wikilink]]` citations
5. If `--file-back` is specified: create a `knowledge/qa/` article and update index.md and log.md

**Why this works without RAG:** At personal knowledge base scale (50-500 articles), the LLM reading a structured index outperforms cosine similarity. The LLM understands what the question is really asking and selects pages accordingly. Embeddings find similar words; the LLM finds relevant concepts.

### 3. Lint (Health Checks)

Seven checks, run periodically:

1. **Broken links** - `[[wikilinks]]` pointing to non-existent articles
2. **Orphan pages** - Articles with zero inbound links from other articles
3. **Orphan sources** - Daily logs that haven't been compiled yet
4. **Stale articles** - Source daily log changed since article was last compiled
5. **Contradictions** - Conflicting claims across articles (requires LLM judgment)
6. **Missing backlinks** - A links to B but B doesn't link back to A
7. **Sparse articles** - Below 200 words, likely incomplete

Output: a markdown report with severity levels (error, warning, suggestion).

---

## Conventions

- **Wikilinks:** Use Obsidian-style `[[path/to/article]]` without `.md` extension
- **Writing style:** Encyclopedia-style, factual, third-person where appropriate
- **Dates:** ISO 8601 (YYYY-MM-DD for dates, full ISO for timestamps in log.md)
- **File naming:** lowercase, hyphens for spaces (e.g., `supabase-row-level-security.md`)
- **Frontmatter:** Every article must have YAML frontmatter with at minimum: title, sources, created, updated
- **Sources:** Always link back to the daily log(s) that contributed to an article

---

## Full Project Structure

```
llm-personal-kb/
|-- .claude/
|   |-- settings.json                # Hook configuration (auto-activates in Claude Code)
|-- .gitignore                       # Excludes runtime state, temp files, caches
|-- AGENTS.md                        # This file - schema + full technical reference
|-- README.md                        # Concise overview + quick start
|-- pyproject.toml                   # Dependencies (at root so hooks can find it)
|-- daily/                           # "Source code" - conversation logs (immutable)
|-- knowledge/                       # "Executable" - compiled knowledge (LLM-owned)
|   |-- index.md                     #   Master catalog - THE retrieval mechanism
```

## Hook System (Automatic Capture)

Hooks are configured in `.claude/settings.json` and fire automatically when you use Claude Code in this project.

### `.claude/settings.json` Format

```json
{
  "hooks": {
    "SessionStart": [{ "matcher": "", "hooks": [{ "type": "command", "command": "uv run python hooks/session-start.py", "timeout": 15 }] }],
    "PreCompact": [{ "matcher": "", "hooks": [{ "type": "command", "command": "uv run python hooks/pre-compact.py", "timeout": 10 }] }],
    "SessionEnd": [{ "matcher": "", "hooks": [{ "type": "command", "command": "uv run python hooks/session-end.py", "timeout": 10 }] }]
  }
}
```

Commands use simple relative paths from the project root. Empty `matcher` catches all events.

### Hook Details

**`session-start.py`** (SessionStart)
- Pure local I/O, no API calls, runs in under 1 second
- Reads `knowledge/index.md` and the most recent daily log
- Outputs JSON to stdout: `{"hookSpecificOutput": {"hookEventName": "SessionStart", "additionalContext": "..."}}`
- Claude sees the knowledge base index at the start of every session
- Max context: 20,000 characters

**`session-end.py`** (SessionEnd)
- Reads hook input from stdin (JSON with `session_id`, `transcript_path`, `cwd`)
- Copies the raw JSONL transcript to a temp file (no parsing in the hook - keeps it fast)
- Spawns `flush.py` as a fully detached background process
- Recursion guard: exits immediately if `CLAUDE_INVOKED_BY` env var is set

**`pre-compact.py`** (PreCompact)
- Same architecture as session-end.py
- Fires before Claude Code auto-compacts the context window
- Guards against empty `transcript_path` (known Claude Code bug #13668)
- Critical for long sessions: captures context before summarization discards it

**Why both PreCompact and SessionEnd?** Long-running sessions may trigger multiple auto-compactions before you close the session. Without PreCompact, intermediate context is lost to summarization before SessionEnd ever fires.

### Background Flush Process (`flush.py`)

Spawned by both hooks as a fully detached background process:
- **Windows:** `CREATE_NEW_PROCESS_GROUP | DETACHED_PROCESS` flags
- **Mac/Linux:** `start_new_session=True`

This ensures flush.py survives after Claude Code's hook process exits.

**What flush.py does:**
1. Sets `CLAUDE_INVOKED_BY=memory_flush` env var (prevents recursive hook firing)
2. Reads the pre-extracted conversation context from the temp `.md` file
3. Skips if context is empty or if same session was flushed within 60 seconds (deduplication)
4. Calls Claude Agent SDK (`query()` with `allowed_tools=[]`, `max_turns=2`)
5. Claude decides what's worth saving - returns structured bullet points or `FLUSH_OK`
6. Appends result to `daily/YYYY-MM-DD.md`
7. Cleans up temp context file
8. **End-of-day auto-compilation:** If it's past 6 PM local time (`COMPILE_AFTER_HOUR = 18`) and today's daily log has changed since its last compilation (hash comparison against `state.json`), spawns `compile.py` as another detached background process. This means compilation happens automatically once a day without needing a cron job or manual trigger.

### JSONL Transcript Format

Claude Code stores conversations as `.jsonl` files. Messages are nested under a `message` key:

```python
entry = json.loads(line)
msg = entry.get("message", {})
role = msg.get("role", "")     # "user" or "assistant"
content = msg.get("content", "")  # string or list of content blocks
```

Content can be a string or a list of blocks (`{"type": "text", "text": "..."}` dicts).

## Script Details

### compile.py - The Compiler

Uses the Claude Agent SDK's async streaming `query()`:

```python
async for message in query(
    prompt=compile_prompt,
    options=ClaudeAgentOptions(
        cwd=str(ROOT_DIR),
        system_prompt={"type": "preset", "preset": "claude_code"},
        allowed_tools=["Read", "Write", "Edit", "Glob", "Grep"],
        permission_mode="acceptEdits",
        max_turns=30,
    ),
):
```

- Builds a prompt with: AGENTS.md schema, current index, all existing articles, and the daily log
- Claude reads the daily log, decides what concepts to extract, and writes files directly
- `permission_mode="acceptEdits"` auto-approves all file operations
- Incremental: tracks SHA-256 hashes of daily logs in `state.json`, skips unchanged files
- Cost: ~$0.45-0.65 per daily log (increases as KB grows)

**CLI:**
```bash
uv run python scripts/compile.py              # compile new/changed only
uv run python scripts/compile.py --all        # force recompile everything
uv run python scripts/compile.py --file daily/2026-04-01.md
uv run python scripts/compile.py --dry-run
```

### query.py - Index-Guided Retrieval

Loads the entire knowledge base into context (index + all articles). No RAG.

At personal KB scale (50-500 articles), the LLM reading a structured index outperforms vector similarity. The LLM understands what you're really asking; cosine similarity just finds similar words.

**CLI:**
```bash
uv run python scripts/query.py "What auth patterns do I use?"
uv run python scripts/query.py "What's my error handling strategy?" --file-back
```

With `--file-back`, creates a Q&A article in `knowledge/qa/` and updates the index and log. This is the compounding loop - every question makes the KB smarter.

### lint.py - Health Checks

Seven checks:

| Check | Type | Catches |
|-------|------|---------|
| Broken links | Structural | `[[wikilinks]]` to non-existent articles |
| Orphan pages | Structural | Articles with zero inbound links |
| Orphan sources | Structural | Daily logs not yet compiled |
| Stale articles | Structural | Source logs changed since compilation |
| Missing backlinks | Structural | A links to B but B doesn't link back |
| Sparse articles | Structural | Under 200 words |
| Contradictions | LLM | Conflicting claims across articles |

**CLI:**
```bash
uv run python scripts/lint.py                    # all checks
uv run python scripts/lint.py --structural-only  # skip LLM check (free)
```

Reports saved to `reports/lint-YYYY-MM-DD.md`.

### memlint.py - Memory Tier Health Checks

`lint.py` stops at `knowledge/`. The files the harness actually injects into every
session live elsewhere and were never audited: `~/.claude/global-memory/` and the
active `~/.claude/projects/*/memory/` slugs. Drift there is the most expensive
drift in the system, because it is read at the start of every conversation.

Seven checks:

| Check | Type | Catches |
|-------|------|---------|
| Index drift | Structural | Memory file missing from MEMORY.md, or an index pointer with no file |
| Broken links | Structural | `[[links]]` that do not match any frontmatter `name:` in the slug |
| Name form | Structural | `name:` that is not the bare kebab stem (type belongs in `metadata.type`) |
| Near-duplicates | Structural | Within-slug TF-IDF similarity above the threshold |
| Cap overruns | Structural | A file past the character cap it declares in its own header |
| Content in index | Structural | Facts written into MEMORY.md, which is meant to hold pointers |
| Contradictions | LLM | Conflicting, redundant, or superseded claims across memory files |

**Scope.** Retired `C--Users-eric-rash*` slugs are excluded everywhere - the macOS
slugs were re-keyed from them, so including them reports history as duplication.
`handoffs/` and `transcripts/` are session records, not memory, and are never linted.
The LLM check defaults to `global-memory` + the `DEV` and `~` slugs, the ones that
load together in a working session; `--all-slugs` widens it.

**Similarity threshold.** Default 0.45. Measured 2026-09-01: the highest genuine
within-slug pair scored 0.33. The report always prints the top pairs per slug so
the number can be retuned against evidence.

**Report only.** memlint never edits a memory file. Merging and deleting memories
stays a human decision.

**CLI:**
```bash
uv run python scripts/memlint.py                    # all checks
uv run python scripts/memlint.py --structural-only  # skip LLM check (free)
uv run python scripts/memlint.py --all-slugs        # widen the LLM check
uv run python scripts/memlint.py --threshold 0.6    # retune near-duplicates
```

Reports saved to `reports/memlint-YYYY-MM-DD.md`; `--structural-only` writes
`memlint-YYYY-MM-DD-structural.md` instead, so a free run never clobbers the
day's paid-for LLM findings. Runs automatically after the Sunday 02:30
adjudication job.

## State Tracking

`scripts/state.json` tracks:
- `ingested` - map of daily log filenames to SHA-256 hashes, compilation timestamps, and costs
- `query_count` - total queries run
- `last_lint` - timestamp of most recent lint
- `last_memlint` - timestamp of most recent memory-tier lint
- `total_cost` - cumulative API cost

`scripts/last-flush.json` tracks flush deduplication (session_id + timestamp).

Both are gitignored and regenerated automatically.

## Customization

### Additional Article Types

Add directories like `people/`, `projects/`, `tools/` to `knowledge/`. Define the article format in this file (AGENTS.md) and update `utils.py`'s `list_wiki_articles()` to include them.

### Obsidian Integration

The knowledge base is pure markdown with `[[wikilinks]]` - works natively in Obsidian. Point a vault at `knowledge/` for graph view, backlinks, and search.

### Scaling Beyond Index-Guided Retrieval

At ~2,000+ articles / ~2M+ tokens, the index becomes too large for the context window. At that point, add hybrid RAG (keyword + semantic search) as a retrieval layer before the LLM. See Karpathy's recommendation of `qmd` by Tobi Lutke for search at scale.

```markdown
# Launchd cloud-push Fails With Operation Not Permitted While Manual Runs Work

The scheduled cloud copy `~/.claude/scripts/cloud-push.py` has failed under launchd at its 07:00 and 17:30 slots since 2026-10-12 18:19, each time with "Operation not permitted". The same script succeeds when run by hand from a terminal; the last good manual runs on 2026-10-14 were 09:13 and 09:17. The script's code is not the problem. The launchd job runs in a different permission context from an interactive shell, and that context is not allowed to read or write the paths the copy touches. On 2026-10-14 the condition was recorded as a Tier A memory file, `project_cloud-push-launchd-blocked.md`, with a matching index line. The interim procedure is to run the copy by hand.

## Key Points

- **"Works by hand, fails on schedule" points to the execution context, not the code.** On macOS, "Operation not permitted" from a launchd job usually means a privacy (TCC) restriction. An interactive terminal holds grants that the background job does not inherit.
- **The interim workaround is a manual run:** `python3 ~/.claude/scripts/cloud-push.py`, then check `~/.claude/scripts/logs/cloud-push.log`. This is an open action item, not a fix.
- **The Full Disk Access fix was deliberately not retried.** A note on file records that it was tried before, so the session followed the note instead of repeating the attempt. The failure stays open.
- **The blocker went into Tier A memory instead of only a handoff,** so every future session on the machine starts knowing the scheduled copy is broken and must not assume Drive holds the latest copy.
- **The two-day gap was visible only in the log.** Nothing else reported it, so the manual-run check is the only evidence that the copy is current.

## Details

This is another case of the process environment being fixed at launch, the failure class seen earlier with Windows Task Scheduler's minimal PATH and with hook environments that differ from the interactive shell. On macOS the difference is about permissions as well as variables. A terminal granted Full Disk Access or access to particular folders passes those grants to scripts it starts. A launchd agent is a separate responsible process and gets none of them. The script is identical, the paths are identical, and the result differs. Running the script by hand cannot reproduce the failure, so a manual success proves only that the code is correct. It says nothing about whether the scheduled job works.

Not retrying the Full Disk Access change is a recorded non-action. Repeating a remedy that a prior note says did not work would cost time and could add confusion about which grant is in effect. Writing the blocker into Tier A memory makes a durable, always-loaded warning in place of a fix. Tier A was used because the consequence is passive: anything that assumes the Drive copy is current, such as a restore or a cross-check, will be quietly wrong until the job works again. The same evening's closeouts ran other jobs cleanly. The 14:14 backup reported status OK, 102 jobs, SSD included. That shows one scheduled job's health says nothing about another's.
```

```markdown
# PP_Recruiting Workbook 012: Benchmark-Tagged Unified Grading

Workbook 012 of the PP_Recruiting project is workbook 010 plus a BENCHMARK tag and a new percentile-profile tab, completed and merged to `main` on 2026-09-26 (PR #2, merge commit `8a3de3a`). It changed no thresholds and no formulas; its purpose is to let per-position grading distributions be read off proven 2025 players. The workbook was staged for staff in `Send\`, and the session recorded three gotchas that must accompany it.

## Key Points

- **Benchmark files contained no new data.** All 710 top-2025 players were already present in the 2025 exports: 578 had zero eligibility remaining (the reason workbook 010 excluded them) and the remaining 132 were already 010 rows.
- **What 012 adds:** a BENCHMARK tag (PORTAL INPUT column BT, REVIEW BOARD column AL) and a final BENCHMARK PROFILES tab giving per-position 25th/median/75th percentiles plus share ≥75, computed live off REVIEW BOARD. Top End Speed is excluded pending mph confirmation. No thresholds or formulas were altered.
- **The data grades proven players low.** Of the 710 proven 2025 players, only 16% project AL or better, about half QS or better, and 78% still flag REVIEW — consistent with an earlier validation run. Mendoza is the exemplar: traits project FRP while a Player Impact of 98 trips REVIEW.
- **012's REVIEW count is inflated by ineligible players.** The displayed 2,352 REVIEW count drops to 010's 1,899 (1,708 with 150+ snaps) once the new Benchmark column is filtered to blank. The 011 screening-matrix numbers still refer to 010, and staff must be told this before opening 012.
- **012 is not loader-safe.** New data keeps loading onto 010, never 012 — the benchmark workbook is a read/analysis artifact, not the ingestion target.
- **Structural grading ceiling at OT/OG/C:** those positions carry only two traits each, so they can only land AA, QS, LIM, or NGE. This is a design consequence of the trait count, not a data defect.

## Details

The benchmark exercise began as an attempt to add proven-player reference data and ended by confirming that no new data existed to add — the value was entirely in tagging and summarizing rows already present. That result matters for interpretation: because the 578 zero-eligibility players were deliberately excluded from 010, tagging them back in for benchmark purposes reintroduces rows that the operational grading view intentionally omits. Hence the inflated REVIEW count and the blank-Benchmark filter that restores the operational numbers. The discipline adopted was to change nothing in the grading logic — no thresholds, no formulas — so that any difference between 010 and 012 is attributable solely to population, not to method. That is what makes the percentile profiles readable as a property of the players rather than of a revised rubric.

The substantive finding is that the grading system rates proven, productive 2025 players low: only 16% project AL or better and 78% still flag REVIEW. Mendoza makes the tension concrete — trait projections land at FRP while a Player Impact score of 98 nonetheless trips REVIEW, meaning the flag is firing on players whose production is close to the ceiling. Read together with the OT/OG/C two-trait ceiling, the pattern suggests the flagging thresholds and the trait coverage per position both need review before the REVIEW flag is treated as a screening signal. Two operational hazards were handled by file hygiene rather than documentation alone: workbook 012 was copied into `Send\` and the stale "Prototype - 003" workbook was moved to `_to_delete\`, so staff cannot open the wrong file. A STATUS correction (`a0cb038`) was pushed immediately after the merge because `main` still claimed 010 as latest, which would have hidden 010–012 from the Mac and from any fresh agent — the same cross-machine staleness problem that the machine-split closeout guards against.

Repository cleanup closed the branch: `worktree-fireflies-review-board-0915` was deleted locally and on GitHub, leaving a single-branch, clean repo. Git released the worktree cleanly, but Windows blocked deletion of the folder itself because Drive sync holds locks on `Desktop\DEV`; Eric cleared it manually, and this is expected on every worktree teardown on this laptop.
```

```markdown
# Flush Outcome Taxonomy: FLUSH_OK, Max-Turns, Version Skew, Session Limit, Network

On 2026-10-10 the memory flush pipeline produced six outcomes across the day. Five were `FLUSH_OK` results (10:32, 11:22, 11:23, 21:43, 21:52). One was a failure at 11:20 reading `FLUSH_ERROR: ResultError: Claude Code returned an error result: Reached maximum number of turns (2) (exit code: 1)`. Max-turns exhaustion was the third distinct failure cause on record, after SDK/CLI version skew and account session-limit exhaustion. On 2026-10-17 a fourth appeared: `API Error: Can't reach the API server — check your internet or DNS (ENOTFOUND) (exit code: 1)` at 20:08. All four are identifiable only from the error text.

## Key Points

- **`FLUSH_OK` is the designed null result, not a failure.** Five of the 2026-10-10 flushes returned it. It means the flush agent read the conversation and found nothing durable worth adding to the daily log.
- **Four causes now share one surface form.** Version skew, session-limit exhaustion, max-turns exhaustion and network/DNS failure all arrive as `FLUSH_ERROR` with exit code 1. Only the message text tells them apart, and each needs a different response: rebuild the pin, wait for the quota reset, accept the loss, or wait for connectivity.
- **"Reached maximum number of turns (2)" is a configuration ceiling, not a defect.** `flush.py` runs the SDK with `max_turns=2`. A session that needs a third turn fails outright and produces no partial result.
- **`ENOTFOUND` is a host-environment failure.** The pipeline and quota were fine, but the machine could not resolve the API hostname. The same DNS error has cut off interactive sessions mid-response (2026-10-02), where "resume" was the whole fix.
- **Each flush outcome describes one session, not the pipeline.** A failure at 11:20 followed by `FLUSH_OK` at 11:22 does not mean the pipeline broke and recovered. It means the two sessions had different content.

## Details

The taxonomy exists because signals that look identical in `.errors.log` and at session start need different responses. A nonzero flush exit always looks like something is broken, but the right action ranges from doing nothing to rebuilding the environment:

- **Version skew:** the bundled CLI has drifted from the system install. Fix it with `uv lock --upgrade-package claude-agent-sdk`.
- **Session limit:** the account quota is spent. The identical retry succeeds after the reset.
- **Network/DNS:** the host had no working connection at the moment the hook fired. Nothing in the stack needs fixing, and a retry succeeds once connectivity is back.
- **Max turns:** the extraction did not fit in two turns. Retrying the same input fails the same way. The only options are raising the ceiling or accepting the loss.

Both quota and network failures are transient on the environment side, but `flush.py` fires once per hook event and does not retry. The cause being transient therefore does not mean the content is recovered. The 2026-10-17 daily log shows this. Its only entry is the 20:08 network failure, and no later flush retried it. The day's daily log, the compiler's source layer, holds no session content at all. Whatever the 20:08 session contained exists only in raw transcripts. Tier B capture serves as the reconstruction fallback here, as it did in the full-day version-skew outage. A "transient" flush failure is a permanent gap unless something goes back and backfills it.

The max-turns case is the quietest of the four. A quota failure clears on its own, and a version failure keeps producing visible errors until it is fixed. A turn-budget failure writes one line and the day continues normally, with nothing to show that a session is missing. The `max_turns=2` ceiling bounds per-session cost, so raising it is a real trade-off. Still, the loss should be visible, which means reading the error text rather than just counting exit codes.

The `FLUSH_OK` results matter for the opposite reason. When "nothing" is often the correct output, that output must be distinguishable from silence. The explicit sentinel provides this: it records that the check ran and found nothing, while an empty append could just as well mean the hook never fired. The same reasoning makes a compile run that produces zero articles a complete result.
```

```markdown
# Stuck Google Drive FUSE Mount: Backup Offline Errors and Hanging Readers

On 2026-10-15 and 2026-10-16 the Mac's daily backup failed with `backup-target-offline:GoogleDrive/_MACHINE`. The local Google Drive mount, a FUSE file layer that shows Drive as a folder, was stuck and did not show `_MACHINE/Backups`. While stuck, any script reading Drive hung: `landed.py scan` and `where-was-i.py --decisions` both had to be stopped and skipped at closeout. This confirms the existing Tier A note `drive-fuse-read-hang`. The same day a storage rulebook, `~/.claude/STORAGE.md`, was written to tell agents where each kind of file belongs.

## Key Points

- **A stuck mount hangs readers; it does not make them fail.** Scripts that list or read Drive block with no error. Without a timeout, a closeout step simply never returns.
- **The backup error points at the mount, not the backup.** `backup-target-offline` here means the local Drive view is stale. The files were reachable through the API, which was used to upload 5 backup files to `_MACHINE/Backups/gws-upload-2026-10-16/`. The code rsync to Drive also finished OK at 16:10.
- **The `.errors.log` entries were kept on purpose,** because the cause was not fixed. They are to be cleared only after a backup succeeds.
- **The open decision is in STATUS:** wait overnight for the mount to recover (recommended), or change the backup to write straight to Google's server instead of the local mount (option 2). The next-morning check is `ls ~/Library/CloudStorage/GoogleDrive-eric.rash11@gmail.com/My\ Drive/_MACHINE`. If `Backups` shows, run `/backup`.
- **Suggested hardening:** a timeout or Drive-offline guard in `landed.py` and `where-was-i.py`.

## Details

Two access paths to the same Drive behaved differently. The API worked: the README fix, closing the Gemini plan and the backup upload all went through it. The FUSE mount did not. Backups and closeout scripts that depend on the mount inherit its health without any sign of it in their own errors, so a backup that looks like it lost its destination is really a local view that stopped updating. Option 2 removes that dependency for backups by writing through the path that was working. The other choice is to wait, on the expectation that a mount refresh will clear the condition.

`STORAGE.md` is the rule side of the same work. It is pointed to from `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` and allowed through the dotclaude `.gitignore` (commit `93c2d8b`), and a safety check was added to `daily-backup.ps1` (`e3f74fa`). The closeout recorded more maintenance debt. Registry drift stands at four items (`Cloudroom_Learning`, `Football/CFB_Playoff_Benchmarks`, `MacEverything`, and Drive `_ACTIVE/2026-10-10_House_Model`). `Cloudroom_Learning` is missing from the backup manifest, which causes the `manifest-unmanaged` error. 1.9 GB of temporary backup files in the session scratchpad are safe to delete. The startup sync skill also committed this session's history file into the dotclaude repo. That breaks the no-history rule, but the file was already tracked, so nothing new was exposed, and the question of how to fix the skill went to STATUS.
```

```markdown
# Connection: Confirmation Must Come From the Layer That Owns the State

## The Connection

Four separate sessions hit the same wall from different directions: the place where a result was *requested* was not the place where the result actually *lived*, so the requesting side could not confirm it. On 2026-07-21 a PR merge appeared to fail because the local main checkout could not swap branches, while the squash-merge had in fact landed on GitHub — the remote owned the state ([[concepts/worktree-remote-merge-verification]]). On 2026-07-18 a background R pull reported exit 1 while its output files sat complete on disk — the filesystem owned the state ([[connections/background-task-exit-code-false-failure]]). On 2026-09-24 a Windows session delegated work to a Mac session that structurally cannot report back, and separately lost the one watch that would have confirmed a Drive upload while being refused permission to look at the folder directly ([[concepts/machine-split-workday-closeout]], [[concepts/background-job-reaped-memory-pressure]], [[concepts/athlete-data-permission-block]]).

## Key Insight

The instinct in all four cases is to trust the nearest available signal — the local checkout, the exit code, the absence of a complaint from the delegated machine — because it is the signal that happens to be in hand. Each of those signals is a *report about* the state rather than the state itself, and each is generated by a layer that does not own the thing being asked about. A local worktree does not own the remote's branch graph; a process's exit status does not own the bytes it wrote; a session on one machine owns nothing on another.

This produces two distinct correct behaviors depending on whether the owning layer is reachable. When it is, query it directly and ignore the proxy: check `gh` or the remote branch, list the output artifacts, read the file. When it is not — a second machine with no return channel, a folder a permission rule forbids listing — the only honest output is an explicitly *unconfirmed* item, paired with the exact command the party who can reach the owning layer should run. The 2026-09-24 handoff does this literally, attaching `launchctl print gui/$(id -u)/com.keystone.dailybackup | grep -A4 -i calendar` to the Mac plist change rather than recording it as done. The failure mode this forecloses is the most expensive one available: a confident false claim of completion, which is strictly worse than an admitted gap because nothing downstream will ever re-check it.

## Evidence

- 2026-07-21: the PR merge "failed" locally because the main checkout owned main; the GitHub squash-merge had landed and synced via fast-forward pull — verify the remote, not the local swap.
- 2026-07-18: a background task's exit-1 notification was a false positive for the SpeedProfiling R pull; reconciliation against on-disk artifacts and logs established success.
- 2026-09-24: "Cross-machine instructions sent to a Mac session cannot report back — anything delegated there is 'unconfirmed' until the user verifies on that machine." The Mac items were written with verification commands attached.
- 2026-09-24: the S2 Drive confirmation was doubly unreachable — the watch job was reaped for memory pressure, and a direct listing was refused because it contained an athlete-named file — and was reported as an unknown rather than inferred.

## Related Concepts

- [[connections/background-task-exit-code-false-failure]] — On-disk artifacts, not the exit code, own task-completion state.

- [[concepts/athlete-data-permission-block]] — A policy boundary can make the owning layer permanently unreachable from a given session.
- [[connections/step-down-to-ground-truth-when-the-surface-lies]] — The complementary principle for when the proxy actively misreports rather than merely being out of reach.
```

```markdown
# `synced (ahead=0)` Does Not Mean Today's Edits Are Committed

A 2026-09-07 config-hygiene session left every edit uncommitted on the expectation that the 09:00 nightly backup would commit and push the skills repo automatically. The session recorded two adjacent status-reading traps: `synced (ahead=0)` reports that nothing is *queued to push*, which is trivially true when nothing has been committed at all; and `com.keystone.dailybackup`'s exit code 1 is stale and clears only on a launchd-initiated run, so manual `/backup` invocations leave it red regardless of outcome.

## Key Points

- **`ahead=0` counts committed-but-unpushed commits.** A working tree full of uncommitted edits produces the same `synced (ahead=0)` as a genuinely clean, fully-backed-up repository — the indicator is blind to the working tree.
- **Deferring commits to the nightly job is a deliberate, defensible choice** (it avoids duplicating the automation's work), but it means the window between the edit and 09:00 has the edits on exactly one disk while the sync indicator reads green. Both of this evening's sessions — the config edits and the `MEMORY.md` trim — were left in that window simultaneously.
- **A stale launchd exit code only clears on a launchd-initiated run.** Manual `/backup` invocations do not reset `com.keystone.dailybackup`'s column-2 status, which stays 1 until the next scheduled tick or an explicit `launchctl kickstart`.
- **The forcing option was named explicitly:** `launchctl kickstart -k gui/$(id -u)/com.keystone.dailybackup` (~7 minutes) versus simply waiting for 09:00. The question was left open with the user rather than decided unilaterally.
- **Unexplained extra runs are worth chasing to a cause.** Additional 07:00 and 07:11 backup runs were resolved as manual user invocations rather than a scheduling defect — a benign explanation, but only after checking.
- **A rollback path was recorded alongside the change:** `git -C ~/.claude checkout CLAUDE.md AGENTS.md .gitignore && rm ~/.claude/TOOLPATHS.md`, with the prior DEV file backed up under the session's job tmp directory.

## Details

The `ahead=0` misreading belongs to the family of status fields whose predicate is narrower than the question being asked of them, described in [[connections/status-field-scope-narrower-than-the-question]]. The field faithfully answers "are there local commits the remote lacks?" and is read as "is my work backed up?" The two coincide only when the working tree is clean, and the deferred-commit workflow adopted here guarantees they diverge for most of the day. The practical consequence is that a durability check must inspect the working tree — `git status`, not the ahead/behind counter — and that the answer to "is today's work safe?" during the deferral window is genuinely no, at least until the CRASHBOX SSD leg captures uncommitted files as documented in [[concepts/on-demand-backup-skill-and-ssd-completeness]]. That leg exists precisely for this class of content, which is why its completeness matters more on days like this one, when a full evening of `~/.claude` and `~/DEV` edits sat uncommitted by design.

The launchd exit-code behavior restates and sharpens the finding from [[concepts/backup-manifest-drift-and-launchd-status-lag]]: column 2 tracks scheduled invocations only. The new detail is the escape hatch — `launchctl kickstart -k` initiates a run *through launchd*, so unlike a manual `/backup` it does update the status field, at the cost of about seven minutes. That gives a genuine choice rather than a resignation: wait for the schedule and let the code self-clear, or force a launchd-initiated run that both commits the day's edits and resets the indicator in one pass. The session correctly framed this as a decision for the user, since the tradeoff is between latency and a few minutes of machine time, not between correct and incorrect.

The extra-runs investigation is a small but instructive counterpoint to the session's other findings. Two unexplained backup executions at 07:00 and 07:11 could plausibly have been a duplicate trigger, a retry loop, or a misconfigured plist — all defects worth fixing. The actual cause was the user running them by hand. The cheapest resolution to an anomaly in a scheduled system is often to ask whether a human caused it, and doing so before instrumenting the scheduler avoids the failure mode where a benign event drives a real change to working automation. Recording the rollback command in the same breath as the change is the complementary habit: it is cheapest to write down while the change set is still in working memory, and it is the only thing that makes an uncommitted, unbacked-up edit set safely reversible.
```

```markdown
# Power Query Formula.Firewall: Structural Fix Over Privacy-Setting Workaround

On 2026-10-02, a Power Query `Formula.Firewall` privacy error in `VB_Revised.xlsx` (the Volleyball_GRID workbook prepared for Baylor volleyball staff member Mike Wenger) was traced to a five-query structure in which `Kinexon Master` both read the raw-data folder *and* consumed results from four helper queries. The immediate remedy — toggling the workbook's "Ignore privacy levels" option — worked but was rejected as the real fix because the setting had already been flipped back off once, likely by the 9:08 save or the 9:10 rename of `VB_Revised_.xlsx` → `VB_Revised.xlsx`. The adopted fix collapsed the five queries into a single self-contained `Kinexon Master` query, removing the condition the firewall reacts to rather than suppressing the reaction. On 2026-10-03 the fix was confirmed on the user's own machine and handed to Mike as paste-ready instructions, leaving only his laptop unverified.

## Key Points

- **The firewall trips on cross-source composition, not on any one source.** `Kinexon Master` mixing a direct folder read with results from four helper queries (Sample File, Transform File, Parameter1, Transform Sample File) is what the privacy firewall blocks; one self-contained query gives it nothing to block. The four helpers were deleted and the rebuild is scripted at `scripts/fix_firewall.ps1`.
- **Per-workbook "Ignore privacy levels" is not durable state.** It can be reset by a save, a rename, or opening the file via a web route, and a user's *global* Excel privacy setting can override it regardless. For a workbook that moves between machines, a settings-based workaround is a recurring failure, not a fix.
- **The test was run with privacy checks on, plus a failing baseline,** and the global setting was checked first to rule out a vacuous pass. On 2026-10-03 the user's own Refresh All on the fixed workbook completed with no errors, which is the second independent confirmation. The expected clean result is ~7,384 rows.
- **The remaining unknown was handed over as a scripted check, not an open question.** `Volleyball_GRID\docs\mike-email-2026-10-02.md` tells Mike to close saved copies, open the file from Box > Kinexon > SandBox in desktop Excel, run Data > Refresh All, read `Ref` tab cell D2 for the local `Kinexon Raw Data` path, and reply with the result — and, if it errors, to screenshot and change nothing. `STATUS.md` was set to "awaiting reply."
- **The branch was pushed but deliberately not merged** pending the user's go-ahead; a concurrent session then merged `fix/firewall-single-query` as PR #2 the following afternoon, and the local branch was cleaned up rather than re-merged.
- **Live-file discipline:** the shared Box copy is never written by tooling; the fixed workbook was produced locally as `workbooks/VB_Revised_firewall-fix.xlsx` and the user performs the copy, rename, and replace.

## Details

The session's governing judgment is that a defect which can be suppressed by a setting is not fixed by that setting when the setting itself is fragile. The evidence was direct: the Box copy already contained the identical query code from the 9/30 repair, so the only thing that had changed was the workbook-level privacy flag, which had reverted — most plausibly during the save or the rename. A fix whose correctness depends on a toggle that the normal file lifecycle resets will fail again on the next save, and will fail invisibly on a second machine whose global privacy preference differs. Collapsing to a single query changes the class of the problem: with no cross-query data flow inside `Kinexon Master`, the firewall has no composition to evaluate, so the privacy setting becomes irrelevant and is retained only as belt-and-suspenders.

The verification design is the second transferable element, and it addresses a specific way confidence can be fabricated. A privacy-firewall fix tested with the firewall bypassed proves nothing, so the run was executed with checks on; and a test that always passes proves nothing either, so a baseline was constructed that reproduced the original error. The pre-check of the *global* Excel privacy option guards the same property from a different direction. Residual uncertainty was then narrowed rather than asserted away: the user's own clean Refresh All on 2026-10-03 added a second environment, and the closest available proxy for Mike's machine was a run with both hardcoded usernames deliberately broken (which passed at 7,384 rows), but the workbook has still never run on Mike Wenger's laptop. The handoff converts that gap into a bounded, scripted report — one path to open the file, one command to run, one cell to read, and an explicit instruction to change nothing on failure. That phrasing matters for a shared live file: an untrained user improvising a fix is the likeliest way to lose the repair.

Two Box Drive quirks surfaced during the work and generalize to any Box-synced Excel project: a 0-byte file usually means Box has not yet downloaded the content locally rather than that the file is empty, and Python cannot open a workbook that Excel currently holds, so a scratch copy is required first. A third, smaller lesson came from the merge instruction the next day. Acting on "merge the branch" without first reading git history would have produced a confusing no-op or a conflicting action, because another concurrent session had already merged `fix/firewall-single-query` as PR #2. When multiple sessions share a repository, the instruction describes an intent whose state must be re-read before acting. Two incidental frictions were also recorded: pushes in `Volleyball_GRID` and `project-triage` print `failed to delete .git/worktrees/...: Permission denied` from stale worktree folders — harmless noise, the pushes succeed — and the global `MEMORY.md` hit its 2,500-character cap, requiring four lines to be shortened before the volleyball thread could be added. A small factual correction was logged: the staff member's surname is Wenger, not Weger.
```

```markdown
# Docker Desktop Uninstall Residue on macOS: Seven Locations

On 2026-09-04 at 07:38, a closeout session revisiting the prior day's Docker Desktop removal found that the first sweep had been incomplete. A wider search located six additional leftover locations across four distinct `~/Library` subdirectories, none of which the original single-path check had covered. All residue was user-owned, requiring no administrator privileges, and the cleanup was verified by searching six separate system paths for any remaining match.

## Key Points

- **Seven locations total,** spread across four `~/Library` subdirectories that a single-path check would not reach: `Preferences/com.electron.dockerdesktop.plist`, `Application Support/com.docker.install`, `Application Support/docker-secrets-engine`, `Caches/Docker Desktop`, `Caches/docker-secrets-engine`, `Application Scripts/group.com.docker`, and `Group Containers/group.com.docker` (already gone).
- **No admin or `sudo` was required** — every leftover was user-owned, which is worth knowing before escalating privileges for a cleanup that does not need them.
- **The bundle identifier is not a reliable search key.** The preferences file is named `com.electron.dockerdesktop.plist` — an Electron-framework identifier — not `com.docker.*`, so a search keyed to the vendor's expected reverse-DNS prefix would miss it.
- **Verification searched six paths, not one:** `~/Library`, the home directory, `/Applications`, `/usr/local`, `/Library/LaunchDaemons`, `/Library/LaunchAgents`, and `/Library/PrivilegedHelperTools`, all returning zero matches. Binaries `docker`, `docker-compose`, and `kubectl` were confirmed absent from PATH.
- **Deletion used `rm` per file followed by `rmdir`,** since the `dcg` guard blocks `rm -rf` outright; `rmdir` refusing non-empty directories made over-deletion structurally impossible.

## Details

The reusable lesson is that a macOS application distributes its state across at least half a dozen conventional locations, and a removal verified against only one of them will report a clean result while leaving most of the residue in place. The four `~/Library` subdirectories involved here — `Preferences`, `Application Support`, `Caches`, and `Application Scripts` — serve genuinely different purposes and are written by different mechanisms, so there is no single parent whose emptiness implies the others are clean. The `Group Containers` and `Application Scripts` entries are particularly easy to overlook because they exist to support app-extension sandboxing rather than the main application, and a user who never knowingly used a Docker extension has no reason to expect them.

The naming observation generalizes beyond Docker. Searching for residue by the vendor's reverse-DNS prefix (`com.docker.*`) is the obvious strategy and would have found five of the seven entries while missing `com.electron.dockerdesktop.plist` entirely, because Electron applications frequently register preferences under the framework's identifier rather than the product's. The robust search key is therefore the *product name* as a substring — which is what the verification pass used, searching for "docker" across all six system paths rather than for any structured identifier. This is the same class of scoping error documented in [[concepts/codex-path-rewrite-incident]], where an initial survey matched only the most obvious shape of a pattern and undercounted the true footprint by roughly eightfold; in both cases the corrective was to enumerate the variant forms before trusting a count.

The cleanup mechanics also record a small safety property. Because the `dcg` guard blocks any command containing `rm -rf`, deletion proceeded file-by-file with `rm` followed by `rmdir` on the emptied directories. `rmdir` fails on a non-empty directory, so an error in the file enumeration would surface as a refusal rather than as silent recursive deletion of unenumerated content — the constrained approach is strictly safer than the one the guard prevented. The session also committed and pushed a related `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` correction (`6ecc6b3`, pushed to `erash11/dotclaude`) updating a `/usr/local/bin` note that the Docker removal had invalidated, and the accompanying handoff was updated to record the `rm` + `rmdir` technique for reuse.
```

```markdown
# Connection: Verify Directly, Don't Trust the Intermediate Layer

## The Connection

Both substantive sessions on 2026-04-22 ran into a version of the same problem: a tool or agent produced output that *looked* fine - a citation with a plausible author list, a photo wired into HTML with a correct relative path - but was actually wrong or unverifiable through the usual checking method. In [[concepts/sportscience-research-repo-batch-import]], a background repair agent's citation fixes for IDs 286, 287, and 358 contained hallucinated author lists despite correctly identifying the papers' topics. In [[concepts/the-monitor-newsletter]], Blake Wright's photo failed to appear in the localhost preview server even though the HTML and file path were both correct.

## Key Insight

In both cases, the fix was not to redo the original work but to change the *verification method* to something closer to the ground truth. The hallucinated citations were caught by extracting the actual PDF text with PyPDF2 and reading it directly, rather than trusting the agent's summarized output. The "broken" photo was confirmed to be fine by opening the HTML file directly in Chrome via `file://`, rather than trusting the brainstorm preview server's rendering. The shared lesson: when an agent, tool, or service produces output that looks plausible but can't be easily double-checked through the same channel, step down to a more primitive, lower-level check (raw file text, direct file rendering) before accepting the result as correct.
```

```markdown
# Connection: Background Task Exit-Code Failures Can Be False Positives

## The Connection

On 2026-07-18, the SpeedProfiling ticket-04 full-game data pull ran as a background R task that reported "failed / exit code 1," yet the task's own log showed a clean end-to-end run — the 10 Hz cache hit, 188 play-by-play plays saved, and the expected outputs written to disk (see [[concepts/speedprofiling-velocity-project]]). This is a specific instance of a recurring class of tooling failure documented across the environment: a status/exit signal reporting failure that does not reflect the actual outcome, where the ground truth lives in a lower-level artifact (a log file, an on-disk output) rather than the reported status code.

## Key Insight

Exit codes and background-task status notifications are intermediate signals, not ground truth. A non-zero exit code from a detached or backgrounded process can be an artifact of the process-management layer (shell wrapper, harness notification, cleanup step) rather than a genuine failure of the work the process performed. The correct diagnostic response is to inspect the actual output — the log's final lines, the files on disk, the row counts — before treating the reported failure as real. On 2026-07-18 the SpeedProfiling pull's on-disk verification (8,932,931 rows for all 61/61 athletes, 69/69 tests passing, both caches confirmed hit on re-run) established the run had actually succeeded despite the exit-1 notification.

This mirrors the memsearch silent `exit 1` failure class (2026-06-13), where a memsearch invocation exited 1 with no surviving diagnostic output — the inverse problem, where a real failure left no trace and could not be diagnosed from the status alone. Together the two cases bracket the same lesson: the exit code and the actual outcome are independent signals that must be reconciled by examining the primitive artifacts. This is the process-execution analog of the broader "verify directly, don't trust the intermediate layer" discipline: just as agent citations, preview-server renders, and retrieval scores can misrepresent ground truth, so can a process's reported exit status.
```

```markdown
# DEV Project Migration to GitHub + Google Drive (Destination-Split Policy)

On 2026-09-14, a staged full-DEV migration moved all Codex and Claude projects to durable remote storage, governed by a destination-split policy that routes each artifact type to GitHub, Google Drive, or neither based on sensitivity and size. The audit at migration start counted 142 local repos with `erash11` remotes, 144 GitHub repos (141 private / 3 public), and none ahead of remote; Google Drive was mounted at `G:\My Drive` with `_DRIVE` mapping to `00_Primary_Storage_Drive`. On 2026-09-24 the policy entered an operational phase: the S2 evaluation data was migrated to Drive and a Parquet-snapshot exchange layer was stood up so two machines could share data without reaching into each other's live working trees.

## Key Points

- **Destination split by artifact type:** code / docs / `AGENTS.md` / `STATUS.md` → GitHub; large datasets, vendor exports, installers, and proprietary files → Google Drive; athlete-identifiable or health data → Drive only (never GitHub); raw conversation transcripts → Drive backup (never in project repos); credentials and `.env` files → neither destination; sanitized memory and handoff summaries → private GitHub context repos.
- **Working repos stay local:** live Git working directories remain under `C:\Users\eric_rash\Desktop\DEV`. Google Drive holds external data and archives, not live working repos.
- **Intentional public/local exceptions:** `Travel_Map`, `SportScienceResearchRepo`, and `JumpReporting` remain intentionally public; `DexaProject` stays local/Drive-only due to sensitive athlete data and is never pushed to GitHub.
- **Codex history not durably backed up:** Codex conversation history is preserved locally under `C:\Users\eric_rash\.codex\sessions\` but is NOT in GitHub and NOT independently backed up off-device — a remaining gap.
- **Raw backups are themselves sensitive:** raw conversation backups contain athlete names, medical context, and historical credentials, so the Drive archive must stay private and unshared — the backup inherits the sensitivity of the most sensitive content it captures.
- **Snapshot exchange, not live cross-reads (2026-09-24):** each pull repo runs `export_snapshot.py` to emit Parquet snapshots that the other machine consumes; the Mac rsyncs `ol_scores.csv` and `team_scores.csv` from `~/DEV/S2_Evaluation/data/` into the Drive S2 folder, and Perch's Windows reads are queued to be repointed at the snapshots rather than at live sources.
- **The Drive-only rule is enforced at the tool layer, and that costs verifiability (2026-09-24):** a direct listing of the S2 Drive folder was refused because the listing itself contains an athlete-named file, leaving the migration's arrival unconfirmed rather than verified.

## Details

The migration's governing principle is that destination is a function of both size and sensitivity, not a single default. Ordinary code and documentation flow to GitHub where version history and collaboration matter; bulky or proprietary binaries (datasets, vendor exports, installers) go to Google Drive to keep repositories lean; and anything athlete-identifiable or health-related is confined to Drive-only storage so it never enters a Git remote at all. Credentials and `.env` files are excluded from both remotes entirely. Sanitized memory and handoff summaries occupy a fourth lane — private GitHub "context repos" — allowing durable, version-controlled continuity documents without exposing raw sensitive material. This mirrors the athlete-data-stays-local convention already established in Baylor's sports-tech pipelines (see [[concepts/kinexon-volleyball-tracking-project]] and [[concepts/speedprofiling-velocity-project]]), where `data/` directories are gitignored so athlete-level data never leaves the machine.

Seven remaining Claude Cowork projects (S2 Cognition, WebApps, PlayerProfiles, StaffProject_BE, Post Season Analysis, UPskilling, PersonalKnowledgeManagement) were queued for migration via a `/migrate-project-to-disk` command and later reported complete in a resume checkpoint pending verification. Several follow-ups remained open: confirming that `Ath_Medicine`, `Baylor_Exposure_Data`, and `Risk_Stratification_Engine` contain no identifiable athlete/health data before their GitHub state is trusted; resolving `_INBOX` changes (a modified `recv.py`, two untracked closeout scripts, and five recovered Python utilities from `agent-skills/_recovered-from-codex/`); a guarded Windows skills v2 sync blocked on an absent `.sync-v2-ready` marker with divergent agent/Codex skill copies to reconcile; and stale documentation (`_INBOX/docs/STATUS.md` still claiming 7 Cowork projects remain, and a stale root "36 `.from-windows` files" item). Optional cleanup included removing a 3.2 GB `C:\Users\eric_rash\Documents\Codex` scratch folder and duplicate clones under `Desktop\DEV\_to_delete\2026-09-14_dup_clones`. Key final commits: DEV router `847bfb9`, `_INBOX` migration handoff `c7e0326`, Claude config `9e807eb`, global memory `b59bf55`, recovered agent utilities `4e00e86`.

The 2026-09-24 machine-split day exercised the policy in two instructive ways. First, once data lives on Drive rather than in a repo, two machines working the same projects need a defined exchange format; the answer adopted was per-repo `export_snapshot.py` runs producing Parquet snapshots, with each host reading the committed snapshot instead of the other host's live data — a read-only, reproducible handoff that keeps the Drive copy authoritative and avoids the divergence problems that plague direct cross-machine reads. Second, the Drive-only rule for athlete data proved to be enforced mechanically and more broadly than the written policy suggests: the permission layer refused a mere *directory listing* of the S2 folder because athlete names appear in file names, meaning identifiable data lives in the metadata as well as the payload (see [[concepts/athlete-data-permission-block]]). No workaround was attempted, so the cost was accepted as an explicit verification gap in the day's handoff — the guardrail behaving correctly, at the price of not being able to confirm from that session that the migration landed.
```

```markdown
# Connection: A Killed Process Leaves Debris That Blocks the Retry

## The Connection

A process that is killed rather than exiting does not run its cleanup path, and what it leaves behind is invisible, persistent, and hostile to the next attempt. On 2026-09-11 an OOM-killed memsearch index left a stale lock file naming a dead PID — and a second such lock, orphaned since August 5, was still present, meaning the condition had silently persisted for over a month. On 2026-07-27, in-session reindex tasks killed twice left orphaned indexer processes holding CPU, requiring manual cleanup. The common finding, stated on 2026-09-11: dead-PID locks are not self-healing.

## Key Insight

The debris is worse than the failure that produced it, because the failure is loud and the debris is silent. An OOM kill is visible — the run stops, the step's duration is anomalous, the operator notices. The lock file it leaves is a small, syntactically valid artifact that the next run reads as a legitimate signal meaning "another indexer is working," so the next run declines politely and logs nothing alarming. The failure mode therefore inverts: a loud crash becomes an indefinitely quiet no-op, and the system reports normal operation while doing none of the work. That one lock survived from August 5 through at least 2026-09-11 is the proof that nothing in the ordinary cycle repairs this; the condition accumulates until someone explicitly checks whether the PID named in the lock is alive.

The structural fix, which none of these cases yet implement, is that any guard file naming a process must be validated against that process's existence before being honoured. A lock is an assertion about the world — "PID 41234 holds this resource" — and assertions about the world go stale exactly when the world moves without notifying the assertion's author. This is the same reasoning that makes an install-time path capture rot silently, and the same reasoning that makes a preservation step require its own verification: a mechanism whose whole purpose is to protect a later operation must be checked, because an unchecked safety net is worse than none. The archive-collision overwrite from 2026-09-09 makes the point from the other direction — there the debris was not a lock but a destroyed file, produced by a cleanup step that assumed a precondition (one archive per day) nothing enforced.

The operational corollary is short: after any kill, enumerate what the killed process owned. Locks, temp files, child processes, partial writes. The kill notification tells you the parent is gone; it tells you nothing about what the parent was holding.

## Evidence

- 2026-09-11 (13:10): the OOM-killed backup left a stale memsearch lock; a second lock orphaned since August 5 was found alongside it. Both would have blocked the next run and were cleared manually, with the explicit lesson recorded that dead-PID locks are not self-healing.
- 2026-07-27 (16:40): foreground memsearch reindex tasks killed twice, each time leaving orphaned indexer processes still consuming CPU that required a manual cleanup pass — a killed parent does not guarantee clean teardown of its children.
- 2026-09-09: a `cp` into a date-keyed archive path destroyed three prior `.errors.log` lines because the cleanup step assumed at most one archive per day; recovered only because git happened to hold a second copy.
```

```markdown
# Connection: Git Infers Repository Boundaries, and Both Directions of That Inference Fail

## The Connection

The 2026-05-20 phantom-changes incident and the 2026-08-15 skills-repo hygiene work look unrelated — one is a stray `git init`, the other is worktree routing and staging discipline. They are the same failure mechanism observed from opposite sides.

Git does not have an explicit notion of "this is my repository." It **infers** the boundary at runtime: walk up from the current directory until a `.git` appears, then treat everything below that point as the tree. Both incidents are that inference producing a boundary nobody intended.

- **Upward, too far:** a `git init` at `C:\Users\eric_rash\` put a `.git` above every project. VS Code's upward walk terminated there instead of at the project root, so 10,000+ files in the user profile presented as untracked changes, and every project-level `.git` under the profile was masked.
- **Downward, too far:** `~/.claude/skills` contained `.claude/worktrees/` holding four live git worktrees. A `git add -A` would have swept their metadata into the tracked tree, embedding repository state inside the repository — the nested-repo condition git handles badly and that is painful to unwind after the commit lands.

One boundary was drawn above where it belonged; one would have been drawn below. Neither was declared — both were inherited from a directory walk.

## Key Insight

The transferable move is that **both fixes work by making the boundary explicit instead of inferred**, and the shape of the fix mirrors the direction of the failure.

For the upward failure, the diagnostic is `git rev-parse --show-toplevel` — literally asking git to state the boundary it inferred rather than trusting the change count that the inference produced. This is the same discipline as [[connections/verify-before-trusting-tool-output]], which both source articles independently cite: the 10,000-change panel and the trim pass's false self-report are both intermediate layers reporting confidently about state they got wrong. Ask for the boundary; don't read it off the symptom.

For the downward failure, the remedy came in two tiers, and the two-tier structure is the reusable part. **Explicit-path staging** — naming every file to stage rather than `git add -A` — fixed it for the commits at hand by refusing to let the tree walk decide. Then `.gitignore` (commit `163db25`) made it structural, so a future session cannot reintroduce it by habit. Tactical control at the moment of action, then a durable constraint so the next actor does not need to remember. The `.claude/worktrees/` gitignore addition explicitly parallels an earlier one made for the same reason in [[concepts/claude-code-worktree-gotchas]] — a repeat is evidence the tactical fix alone does not hold.

There is a sharper lesson in the asymmetry of consequences, which is why the two incidents warrant different levels of caution despite the shared mechanism. The home-directory `.git` was **trivially reversible**: the diagnostic check — no refs, no `COMMIT_EDITMSG`, no `packed-refs` — confirmed the init had produced nothing, so deletion lost no work. A committed nested worktree is not reversible in the same cheap way; it enters history, propagates on the daily cross-machine sync, and has to be surgically removed. This is precisely why the skills repo carries heavier machinery — worktree-routed edits under a background-isolation guard, credential scans, diff review before committing — while the home-directory case needed only a check and an `rm`. The prevention investment should scale with how hard the boundary error is to undo once written, not with how alarming it looks when discovered. The 10,000 phantom changes were the loud, harmless case; the four nested worktrees were the quiet, expensive one.

That same asymmetry generalizes to the wider repo-lineage lesson in [[concepts/committed-symlink-repo-landmine]]: what gets *committed* is where cheap mistakes become expensive ones, which is the reason to spend effort at the staging boundary rather than after the fact.

## Evidence

- 2026-05-20 (12:25): VS Code showed 10,000+ pending changes at instance open, before any edits. Root cause was `git init` at `C:\Users\eric_rash\`; the `.git` was a bare skeleton with no commits, stashes, refs, or remote, confirmed safe to delete. # Launchd cloud-push Fails With Operation Not Permitted While Manual Runs Work
```

The scheduled cloud copy `~/.claude/scripts/cloud-push.py` has failed under launchd since 2026-10-12 18:19, each time with "Operation not permitted". The same script succeeds when run by hand from a terminal. The code is not the problem: the launchd job runs in a different permission context from the interactive shell. A 2026-10-21 investigation narrowed the cause further. The job runs a different Python from the shell, and the macOS privacy layer (TCC) lets that Python read the Google Drive CloudStorage folder but not write to it. The fix is to grant Full Disk Access to the exact binary the job runs, `/usr/bin/python3`. That is a manual step for Eric in System Settings, and it was still pending at the end of the session.

## Key Points

- **"Works by hand, fails on schedule" points to the execution context, not the code.** An interactive terminal holds TCC grants that a launchd job does not inherit.
- **Reads can succeed while writes fail.** On 2026-10-21, `ls` on the Drive folder worked, but writes to `My Drive/_MACHINE/Cloud_Copy/DEV/` failed with `Operation not permitted`. A working read does not show that the job can write.
- **The job and the shell use different interpreters.** The job `com.keystone.clouddrivepush` runs `/usr/bin/caffeinate -i /usr/bin/python3 /Users/kristinarash/.claude/scripts/cloud-push.py`. The shell's `python3` is Homebrew `/opt/homebrew/opt/python@3.14/bin/python3.14`. Full Disk Access has to go to `/usr/bin/python3`, the binary the job actually executes.
- **`launchctl print ... | grep -i program` shows only `caffeinate`.** The real interpreter and script are listed in the `arguments` block, so read the whole block.
- **The blocker sits in Tier A memory** (`project_cloud-push-launchd-blocked.md`), so every session knows the Drive copy may not be current. Manual runs remain the interim workaround.

## Details

This failure belongs to the class where the process environment is fixed at launch, the same class as Windows Task Scheduler's minimal PATH and hook environments that differ from the interactive shell. On macOS the difference covers permissions as well as variables. A terminal with Full Disk Access passes that grant to the scripts it starts. A launchd agent is a separate responsible process and starts with none of it. The script and paths are identical but the outcome is not, so a manual success proves only that the code is correct.

The 2026-10-21 session added three facts. First, failures continued at 2026-10-20 17:46 and 2026-10-21 07:33, and a manual `launchctl kickstart` also exited 1. Kickstart runs the job inside launchd's context, so it reproduces the failure, which a terminal run cannot do. That makes kickstart the right test once the fix is in. Second, the read/write split shows the denial is specific to the operation, so a read-only probe gives a false all-clear. Third, the interpreter mismatch explains why earlier Full Disk Access attempts could have appeared to do nothing: a grant to the Homebrew Python, or to the terminal, never reaches `/usr/bin/python3`. Permissions were deliberately not changed from the shell. The handoff is a short scripted procedure: add `/usr/bin/python3` under System Settings > Privacy & Security > Full Disk Access, run `launchctl kickstart -k gui/$(id -u)/com.keystone.clouddrivepush`, then confirm with `tail -5 ~/.claude/scripts/logs/cloud-push.log`.

The same session restored `~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.keystone.dailybackup-login.plist`, which Eric had deleted with `rm`. The copy in `~/.claude/scripts/` was put back and bootstrapped only after Eric's own explicit approval. The job loaded with last exit code 0, but the backup itself was not run.

## Related Concepts

- [[connections/manual-run-success-does-not-validate-scheduled-context]] - Why the test has to be a kickstart inside launchd, not a terminal run.
- [[connections/a-probe-must-match-the-jobs-binary-and-operation]] - The `ls`-versus-write and shell-versus-job-Python mismatches, viewed as one probe-design error.
- [[concepts/relayed-instructions-are-not-user-consent]] - The consent rule followed for the plist restore and the Drive write.
- [[concepts/mac-evening-machine-schedule-split]] - The earlier Mac scheduler changes this job sits alongside.
- [[concepts/claude-code-memory-architecture]] - Why a blocker with passive consequences goes to Tier A.

# PP_Recruiting Workbook 027: Mauro's Telemetry Metric Suggestions

Workbook 027 of the PP_Recruiting grading project was built on 2026-10-21 from 026 TEST. It adds four groups of metric changes that Baylor assistant GM Anthony Mauro proposed by email, drawing on Telemetry data. 026 TEST already included Mauro's earlier answers and passed every check. The 027 build kept the REVIEW board at 2,852 rows, the same as 026, which is the expected invariant. A checker run on 027 was still in progress when the session's log ended, so the workbook had not yet been verified, committed, or sent.

## Key Points

- **Athleticism:** add Change of Direction (CoD) to Quickness; replace Adjusted Speed with Power Speed for TE, ILB, CB and SAF; add Power Speed to RB Speed. Mauro's reasoning was that Power Speed measures athletic ability, while Adjusted Speed measures effort and motor.
- **On-field performance:** add Rushing Effectiveness, Receiving Effectiveness and Run Stops Over Expected, and align each metric more closely with the trait it is meant to measure.
- **IDL and EDGE:** add Disruption and Double Team Rate. Disruption (how quickly a player gets vertical) stays separate from Get Off, which also reflects situational instinct.
- **Player Impact (tWAR)** is added as an overall value measure covering availability, playing time and effective production. It supplements the trait grades and does not replace them.
- **The REVIEW row count is the regression check.** After a version bump it should stay at 2,852. A change there means the build broke something, not that the metric logic changed.

## Details

Getting the input took a manual step. Gmail held only a WeTransfer notice that Mauro had downloaded 026. His reply was most likely in Baylor Outlook, which Claude cannot read, so Eric pasted the email text into the chat. Claude then wrote a build script, changed the checker so it could validate 027, and built the workbook. The suggestions separate what a metric measures from how it is labeled: Power Speed versus Adjusted Speed is ability versus effort, and Disruption versus Get Off is raw quickness versus quickness plus instinct. They also fit the earlier benchmark finding that the grading rated proven players low, a gap a production-based tWAR measure is intended to cover.

Two build-level lessons came out of the session. Raw XLSX XML can contain empty `<v/>` value tags, and a cell-reading regex that assumes `<v>…</v>` fails the build on them. The scripts were also changed so row references start at row 5, which makes spreadsheet-style references like `BL5` work in both the build and the checker. Open items: get the 027 checker result and fix any failures, update `PP_Recruiting/docs/STATUS.md` from 026 to 027 and push it (a stale STATUS on `main` previously hid new workbooks from the other machine), then send 027 to Mauro or Anthony once it passes.
